notes: No parties in Nauru in 1970 (Nauru Party 1976, DPN 1987 - MD's DPN in slot 15 is anachronistic and not used). Ruling slot 2 holds the Nauru Local Government Council, the body Head Chief Hammer DeRoburt led to independence. Coalition slot 1 holds the Nauru Congregational Church as the main conservative force. Slot 0 = British Phosphate Commissioners (until the 1 July 1970 handover). Slot 23 = Temonibe chiefly rank.

0.name: British Phosphate Commissioners
0.text:
The British Phosphate Commissioners, the board appointed by the governments of Britain, Australia and New Zealand, have mined Nauru's phosphate since 1920 and still run the works under an agreement that transfers them to Nauruan ownership on 1 July 1970. Their managers, Australian staff and Chinese and Gilbertese contract labourers make up much of the island's population.

The Commissioners represent Western economic control: cheap fertiliser for Australian and New Zealand farms, continuity of operations and minimal interference from Nauruan politics. They resisted full Nauruan ownership and refuse responsibility for rehabilitating the mined land. Until the handover their leverage is overwhelming: they control the island's only industry, its port facilities, power and much of its housing.

1.name: Nauru Congregational Church
1.text:
The Nauru Congregational Church descends from the Protestant mission that Philip Delaporte brought to the island in 1899, and most Nauruans belong to it. Its pastors, deacons and women's fellowships are woven into every district, and much of the island's political class worships in its congregations.

The church upholds Christian morality, family and community discipline, Sunday observance and the Nauruan language through its Bible and hymnal. It is pro-Western and anti-communist, and generally supports the government while urging that phosphate wealth be used responsibly. Its leverage is moral: it shapes opinion in a small, close community where nearly everyone attends church.

2.name: Nauru Local Government Council
2.text:
The Nauru Local Government Council, created in 1951 and led by Head Chief Hammer DeRoburt since the 1950s, is the institution that won Nauru's independence on 31 January 1968. DeRoburt, now President of the Republic, governs through the councillors and members of Parliament who campaigned with him against the trusteeship powers and the British Phosphate Commissioners. Formal political parties do not exist.

The council's programme is national ownership of the phosphate industry, due on 1 July 1970, the investment of royalties for the day the deposits run out, and rehabilitation of mined land. It is pro-Western in alignment but fiercely protective of Nauruan sovereignty. Its leverage lies in DeRoburt's authority and the island's new wealth.

3.name: The Fair Share
3.text:
The Fair Share is the demand, heard among Nauruan clerks, teachers and younger islanders, that phosphate wealth should benefit every Nauruan and not only those whose family land happens to lie on the richest deposits. It has no organisation, but the argument surfaces in Parliament, in district meetings and in the Local Government Council.

Its advocates want royalties shared more equally, free housing, health care and education for all citizens, scholarships abroad and a welfare state financed by the phosphate industry. They are pro-Western and admire the social programmes of the Australian Labor Party. Their leverage lies in the egalitarian instincts of a community of only a few thousand Nauruans.

4.name: Itsio
4.text:
Itsio, the name of the lowest of Nauru's traditional ranks, is taken up by a small circle of young commoners and returned students who have read Marxist literature in Australia and met members of the Communist Party of Australia and the Waterside Workers' Federation. There is no communist organisation on the island; the circle exists in conversation and imported pamphlets.

Its members argue that the phosphate industry should be run by and for working people, that chiefly rank and private royalties perpetuate inequality, and that the Soviet Union shows small nations a path free of Western capital. They are isolated, but the gulf between rich landowners and the landless gives their arguments a hearing.

5.name: Young Naoero
5.text:
Young Naoero is the outlook of Nauruan students returning from secondary schools and colleges in Australia, where they have seen anti-war marches and Aboriginal rights campaigns in Melbourne and Sydney. They come back to an island run by elders and a single dominant leader, where phosphate money arrives faster than any plan to use it.

They want a more open and accountable government, solidarity with decolonisation across the Pacific, criticism of Australian and Western mining interests, and a share of power for the young. They have no organisation beyond student and church youth groups. Their leverage is their education: the new republic needs their skills to run itself.

6.name: The Twelve Tribes
6.text:
The Twelve Tribes speaks for clan heads and elders who measure everything by the twelve traditional clans commemorated in the twelve-pointed star of the national flag. They distrust the Australians, the Phosphate Commissioners and the European ways that mining brought, and they remember the wartime Japanese deportations that nearly destroyed their people.

They want clan authority restored in land matters and public life, foreign workers and influences kept to a minimum, and Nauruan custom placed above Western law and consumer habits. They are hostile to Australian tutelage and would welcome any partner that respects Nauruan pride. Their leverage lies in land: every mining lease needs the consent of Nauruan landowning families.

7.name: Yaren Inner Circle
7.text:
The Yaren Inner Circle is the small group of ministers, officials and confidants who surround President Hammer DeRoburt in the government offices at Yaren. In a parliament of eighteen members without parties, they manage majorities, appointments and the flow of phosphate revenue, and they expect to control the state corporation being prepared to take over the mines.

They favour strong presidential government, minimal opposition and a foreign policy that bargains hard with Australia while looking to Japan and other Asian markets and partners. They regard criticism as disloyalty to the nation that fought for independence. Their leverage rests on DeRoburt's personal dominance and on their command of the state's purse.

8.name: Halqat Ahl al-Bayt
8.text:
Halqat Ahl al-Bayt is a handful of Muslim seamen and contract workers who pass through Nauru on phosphate ships and occasionally meet for prayer in their quarters; a few follow Shia teaching learned from Khoja communities in East Africa and India. Nauru has no mosque and no Muslim community of its own.

The circle shares the reformist Shia outlook associated with Musa al-Sadr in Lebanon: faith joined to social justice, education and the dignity of the poor, pursued within existing law. It has no political ambitions on the island. Its only relevance lies in the threads of contact it maintains with the wider Muslim world.

9.name: Ansar al-Najaf
9.text:
Ansar al-Najaf is the name a few transient Shia believers give to their loyalty to Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, the exiled Iranian cleric whose lectures on Islamic government circulate from Najaf. On Nauru they are almost invisible: crewmen on ore ships and occasional labourers with recordings and pamphlets from the Gulf.

They hold that legitimate rule belongs to the Islamic jurist, condemn both American and Soviet power, and see Western mining of small nations' resources as plunder. They have no Nauruan followers. Any influence would depend on a revolution in the Muslim heartlands that gives their cause money, prestige and a state to back it.

10.name: Rabitat al-'Alam al-Islami
10.text:
The Muslim World League, founded in Mecca in 1962 under Saudi royal patronage, funds mosques, literature and scholarships for Muslim communities worldwide and reaches the Pacific mainly through Fiji and Australia. On Nauru its influence is limited to literature sent to the few Muslims among foreign workers and visiting crews.

The League preaches a Saudi-sponsored orthodoxy: obedience to Muslim rulers, strict monotheism, rejection of communism and secular nationalism, and alignment with the West against Soviet influence. It works through institutions rather than parties. Its leverage is money: any Muslim community that took root on the island would look to it first for funding.

11.name: Da'wat al-Khilafa
11.text:
Da'wat al-Khilafa is the idea of a restored caliphate as spread by Hizb ut-Tahrir pamphlets that reach a few Muslim students at universities in Australia and Fiji. On Nauru it has no following; its literature surfaces only occasionally among foreign workers on the island.

The circle rejects republics, monarchies and democracy alike as man-made systems, and calls for a single Islamic state under one caliph that would end both Western and Soviet domination and the plunder of Muslim resources. It is secretive and hostile to established Muslim leaders. On a Christian island it has no leverage beyond the curiosity of a few individuals.

12.name: Fiji Muslim League
12.text:
The Fiji Muslim League, founded in 1926 by Indo-Fijian Muslims, runs mosques, schools and welfare work across Fiji and is the leading Muslim body in the South Pacific. Fijian clerks, tradesmen and teachers working on Nauru on contract give it a thin thread of contact with the island.

The League combines religious education with community uplift and peaceful participation in politics, influenced by the revivalist currents of South Asian Islam. It is anti-communist and works within the institutions of the state. On Nauru it has no presence beyond individual contacts; its leverage lies in Fiji, where Indo-Fijians now outnumber indigenous Fijians.

13.name: Nauru Phosphate Royalties Trust
13.text:
The Nauru Phosphate Royalties Trust, established in 1968, invests the share of phosphate earnings set aside for the day when Nauru's deposits are exhausted. Its trustees and their Australian advisers manage a growing portfolio of property, bonds and shares abroad, and it is already the most important economic institution of the republic besides the mines themselves.

The Trust embodies a technocratic, non-aligned vision of the state: Nauru as a self-financing rentier nation investing wherever returns are highest, from Melbourne to Asia and the Pacific. Its managers prefer discretion to parliamentary scrutiny. Its leverage is financial: it holds the nation's future income and decides how it is spent.

14.name: Catholic Church in Nauru
14.text:
The Catholic Church in Nauru dates from the Missionaries of the Sacred Heart who arrived in 1902 and is the island's second Christian community. It is administered from the diocese based at Tarawa in the Gilbert Islands, and its priests also minister to many of the Gilbertese and Tuvaluan contract workers in the phosphate settlements.

The church stands for Catholic social teaching, family life, education through its schools and charity toward the poorer workers of the phosphate economy. It is non-partisan and avoids taking sides between factions, but warns against materialism as royalties transform island life. Its leverage lies in its schools and in its standing among workers and a substantial minority of Nauruan families.

15.name: The Royalty Holders
15.text:
The Royalty Holders are the Nauruan families whose land lies on the richest phosphate fields of Topside, the island's raised interior. Every tonne mined from their plots brings them direct royalty payments, and as Nauruan control of the industry approaches they stand to become wealthy by any standard. Their heads sit on the Council, in Parliament and on public boards.

They want royalties paid to individual landowners rather than pooled by the state, low taxation, freedom to spend and invest their earnings as they wish, and influence over leases and contracts. They are pro-Western by habit and comfortable with Australian banks. Their leverage lies in land ownership, without which no phosphate can be mined.

16.name: Aiwo Traders
16.text:
The Aiwo Traders are the shopkeepers, contractors and small businessmen clustered around the port and phosphate works in Aiwo district: Chinese storekeepers, Nauruan families opening shops and transport services, and Australian agents of trading firms. As royalty money spreads, demand for imported goods, cars and services grows every month.

They want free enterprise, few licences and tariffs, open access to imports and freedom from public monopolies such as the Cooperative Society and the planned state corporations. They favour Australia and the West as trading partners. Their leverage lies in supplying an island that produces almost nothing but phosphate.

17.name: Restore the Topside
17.text:
Restore the Topside is the cause of Nauruans who look at the mined-out interior of their island, a wasteland of coral pinnacles where forest and food trees once grew, and demand that it be made habitable again. The Local Government Council has pressed this claim against the trusteeship powers for years, and families raise it whenever royalties are discussed.

Its supporters want the British Phosphate Commissioners and their governments to pay for rehabilitating land mined before independence, revenue reserved for restoring the land and limits on mining that leaves nothing behind. It is anti-colonial and non-aligned. Its leverage lies in legal claims and international sympathy at the United Nations.

18.name: Nauru Cooperative Society
18.text:
The Nauru Cooperative Society, founded in 1923 by Timothy Detudamo, is the islanders' own trading enterprise, created to break the hold of the phosphate company's stores. Owned by its Nauruan members, it runs the main retail shops and returns its profits to the community.

The Society embodies a Nauruan cooperative ideal: collective ownership, fair prices, member dividends and economic self-reliance against foreign commercial interests. It is non-aligned and community-minded, distrustful of both private traders and distant governments. Its leverage lies in supplying much of the island's food and goods, and in the loyalty of the families who have built it over nearly half a century.

19.name: Hongqi Xiaozu
19.text:
Hongqi Xiaozu is a small circle among the Chinese contract workers recruited from Hong Kong to labour in the phosphate works. Some arrived after the leftist riots in Hong Kong in 1967 and carry Mao Zedong's Quotations, mainland newspapers and the language of the Cultural Revolution into the workers' quarters at Location.

The group denounces the British Phosphate Commissioners as imperialists, demands equal pay and housing for Chinese and Pacific labourers, and praises self-reliance on the Chinese model. It opposes Soviet revisionism as firmly as Western capitalism. Its members cannot vote or hold office, but the mines depend on their labour, and strikes are their only weapon.

20.name: Angam
20.text:
Angam takes its name from the national day of 26 October, which celebrates the Nauruan population regaining fifteen hundred people, the number held necessary for survival, a recovery repeated after the wartime Japanese deportations. The faction speaks for Nauruans who see their people as a fragile minority on their own island.

It calls for strict limits on foreign residents, priority for Nauruans in every job and contract, the eventual departure of contract workers and Australian staff, and laws protecting Nauruan identity. It is pro-church and anti-communist but resents Australia. Its leverage lies in a deep anxiety about national survival that every Nauruan family shares.

21.name: Naoero Guard
21.text:
Naoero Guard is the name some young Nauruan men give to their idea of a disciplined national corps to defend the island and keep order among its foreign workers. Nauru has no army, and they resent that its defence and much of its police training still depend on Australia.

They want a uniformed national force, firm control over contract labourers, punishment for those who offend Nauruan honour and a leader who rules without parliamentary delays. They glorify the endurance of the wartime deportees and despise compromise with outsiders. They have no organisation and no recognised leader; their leverage would come only from unrest in the workers' settlements.

22.name: Nauru Police Force
22.text:
The Nauru Police Force is the only uniformed body of the republic, a small force of Nauruan and Pacific Islander officers responsible to the President's government. It keeps order in the districts, the port and the crowded workers' settlements, and Australian officers still help with training and advice.

The force is loyal to the government and politically quiet, but it is the only armed instrument available in a crisis, whether a strike in the phosphate works or a clash among contract labourers. Its commanders value order, discipline and the authority of the state over political bargaining. Its leverage is small, but no rival armed body exists.

23.name: Temonibe
23.text:
Temonibe was the highest rank of traditional Nauruan society, the chiefly families who led the clans before German and Australian rule hollowed out their authority. Under the Australian administration a Council of Chiefs survived until 1951, and Hammer DeRoburt still bears the title of Head Chief through the Local Government Council.

The temonibe families and their followers want the chiefly hierarchy honoured in national life, land disputes settled by customary authority and leadership reserved for those of proper descent. They are conservative, Christian and wary of both foreign workers and new money. Their leverage is limited to prestige, ceremony and their role in arbitrating land and family matters.
